{"id": "4ad37f3b-46d0-41a9-a948-e9ae7d0c7173", "value": "{\"id\": \"1d5c7e2c-971b-40a5-8979-79c24477849b\", \"value\": \"Of the two lithic technologies that characterise the Early Stone Age (ESA) elsewhere in Africa\u2014\n Oldowan and Acheulean\u2014only the latter has been clearly documented in the Senegambia\"}"}

{"id": "893309fd-c533-401a-8e0a-2a960007be59", "value": "{\"id\": \"ad4e4cbf-71d7-453b-aecf-d4fd4caef827\", \"value\": \"Description: \"The ceramics of the Wind\u00e9 Koroji tradition are characterized by numerous shallow cauldrons and tighly closed jars both featuring everted rims (fig. 4a-c). Alo distinctive but much less common are broad basins (fig. 4d). Open bowls and globular simple rimmed vessels are also present (fig. 4e-f). The most common decors are twisted twine roulettes (Twisted Tw) impressed or roulette cord-wrapped stick (ICS/CSR) and impressed netting (Net/Fabric) (Table 1). The latter motif is especially striking occurring both tightly applied to the vessel and loosely impressed. Highly distinctive but less common decor types include knotted twine roulettes (often featuring multiple knots) (fig. 4c) braided twine roulette (which produce a \"herringbone effect\") and a curious type of \"applied\" plastic decor. This latter motif features the semi-perforation of the pot with a blunt tipped object and a subsequent re-finishing of resultant voids and bulbs (fig. 4d). \" The site of Wind\u00e9 Koroji Ouest (WKO) the type site of the facies is located at the centre of the Wind\u00e9 Koroji complex in the vicinity of a seasonal Songhai hamlet. | Description: \"Le faci\u00e8s de Wind\u00e9 Koroji bien qu'apparent\u00e9 aux faci\u00e8s n\u00e9olithiques de la vall\u00e9e du Tilemsi offre plusieurs particularit\u00e9s. Il se caract\u00e9rise au niveau de la c\u00e9ramique par des formes en \"chaudrons\" peu profonds et des jarres \u00e0 ouverture r\u00e9duite. La plupart des bords sont assez \u00e9vers\u00e9s. Les poteries sont en r\u00e8gle g\u00e9n\u00e9rale d\u00e9graiss\u00e9es \u00e0 la chamotte et d\u00e9cor\u00e9es au peigne filet\u00e9 souple \u00e0 la cordelette roul\u00e9e ou bien encore par impression de nattes ou de filets. L'industrie lithique est tr\u00e8s particuli\u00e8re. Les armatiures de fl\u00e8ches salicyforme ou foliac\u00e9es en silex pr\u00e9dominent au c\u00f4t\u00e9 d'une industrie grossi\u00e8re sur gr\u00e8s. Les haches polies de tailles variable sont aussi pr\u00e9sentes. Les sondages sir me soye de Wind\u00e9 Koroji ont r\u00e9v\u00e9l\u00e9 deux structures pratiquement affleurante : le fond d'une hutte circulaire et une petite fosse remple de mat\u00e9riel. Les restes de faune comprennent des bovins des ovicaprins un grand nombre de mammif\u00e8res sauvages et des poissons adapt\u00e9s aux eaux peu profondes. Les meules sont abondantes. Les restes de pal\u00e9oflore ont livr\u00e9 des esp\u00e8ces sauvages et quelques graines de Pennisetim sp. vraisemblablement domestique. Une \u00e9conomie pastorale semble pouvoir \u00eatre rattach\u00e9e au faci\u00e8s Wind\u00e9 Koroji. \"\"}"}

{"id": "0e88bab5-0420-4a63-9b68-8f7a73c155b7", "value": "Description: The Kobadi tradition would appear to have been of an entirely fisher-hunter-gatherer economic orientation and has been documented in the Malian Sahara and throughout most of the Middle Niger and Niger bend area (e.g. Raimbault and Dutour 1989; Togola and Raimbault 1991; MacDonald and Van Neer 1994; MacDonald 1996b; Raimbault 1996). Kobadi ceramics differ greatly from those of Tichitt having entirely different rim forms (simple rather than everted) decorative tools (comb and spatula rather than cordwrapped stick) and fabric (sand and sponge temper rather than chaff)."}

{"id": "8c22ce2a-cb23-4bef-9bba-55d26782ffac", "value": "{\"id\": \"73b71b9b-b341-4442-ab88-0ae473cec133\", \"value\": \"Description: \"he Middle assemblage from approximately AD 200-1000 was the most diverse and widepsread having been recovered from Fati4 Fati6 Fati7 and Fati9. Everted rim vessels with ribbing/channelling and red slip were the most numerous examples. These vessels were also burnished in small but significant numbers. Rocovered at both Gao Ancien and Tombouze these are characteristic of assemblage dating to the second half of the fisrt millenium AD (Insoll 2000; Park 2012). Other burnished wares with geometric comb impressions with a 'checkerboard' pattern of slipped and unslipped areas from the Ghourma Rharous Middle assemblage have been found around Lake Fabuibine (IFAN-MAL-55-39-4). Triangular or arced comb impressions over red burnished surfaces have been found at Djim-Djim (IFAN-MAL-55-45) El Oualadji and Killi (Lebeuf & Paques 1970: 28) and in the Gourma-Rharous (McIntosh & McIntosh 1985). These burnished comb-impressed sherds are potentially examples of the terminal Middle phase as they have been elsewhere dated to the turn of the second millennium AD (McIntosh & McIntosh 1985: 35).\"\"}"}

skos:Concept.skos:scopeNote: {"id": "64337d4c-cc2d-47cc-aa13-307a06b284c4", "value": "A clay-based product, usually divided into pottery (such as earthenware, stoneware, and faience) and porcelain (soft-paste, hard-paste, and bone china). Excavated ceramics can be used for relative dating to give an approximate date range for a site. Any relative dating technique requires accurate identification. Site occupation dates derived from excavated ceramics must be used with caution and preferably in conjunction with other sources of evidence. Example: In the MAEASaM Chronological Type, the Ceramic class is classified into 5 broad sub-categories. For example: eathernware (generally pertaining to hand-made or thrown clay vessels). Earthenware includes local pottery manufactured on-site but can also relate to earthenware that has been imported through trade networks or other historical events. In some cases, a particular temper used during the firing of vessels can be used as a distinguishable marker for a particular time period. For example, charcoal, grog, quartz, silcrete, shell, bone, etc."}

{"id": "d8dc191a-5eb7-4bee-847e-21f59c7dd622", "value": "This Neolithic stream is characterised by macrolithism and microlithism cut on quartz and flint. The deposits also provide ceramics decorated with impressions and degreased with lateritic gravel chamotte sand and quartz."}

{"id": "d42fb6b5-2b48-48db-8db8-bb87b5921847", "value": "Contentious chronological term referring to a type of pottery characterised by the use of several different wavy line decorations with additional dot marks between them found both in the Nile Valley and across the wider Sahel-Sahara belt. Assumed to be a successor to the Wavy Line by early researchers (e.g. Arkell) associated with the Khartoum Neolithic vs Khartoum Mesolithic but proven to be found in Khartoum Mesolithic/Neolithic occupations from beginning to end and found earlier than the Wavy Line in Sahara-Sahel contexts. Chronological associations have yet to be fully deciphered but current estimates suggest 10000BP - 4000BCE."}

{"id": "8bb4afac-0c83-4344-a48b-273780d3871f", "value": "The period immediately prior to the emergence of the Aksumite Kingdom. Material evidence of this period including ceramics and funerary monuments are already Aksumite in style but have distinctive traits from later Aksumite ones. This includes stone platforms associated with stelae and pit graves. In the Later Proto-Aksumite phase the monoliths become larger in size. Proto-Aksumite ceramics are characterized by very fine and hard farbrics mostly orange ware with decoration being rare.Flaked stone tool industry continues to be present along with evidence of domestic livestock including cattle sheep and goats and Near Eastern domestic crops including emmer wheat free-threshing wheat barley lentil and linseed/flax and with less certainty the Ethiopian/Eritrean domesticated crop of tef (t'ef). Included in this time phase is the presence of imported glass beads with possible origins to Ptolemaic Egypt. It was also during this time period which saw the increase of Egyptian activity on the African Red-Sea coast. The Ptolemaic dynasty of Macedonian-descended Kings who ruled Egypt from the end of the 4th century BC actively sought African war elephants mounting expeditions along the Red Sea for that purpose.Funerary evidence suggests contacts with the Kingdom of Kush (Napata/Meroe) in the Middle Nile Valley of Suday. Iron and bronze (although not in frequency) indicate links with Meroitic and Post-Meroitic Kingdoms of the late 1st Millennium BC and mid-1st Millennium AD. The origins of the Aksumite Kingdom might be traced directly back to this phase particularly at Beta Giyorgis hill. Debate exists over the end of the Proto-Aksumite period. Fattovich (2010) suggests at 40 BCE end date and Phillipson (2012) suggests at date of around 120 BCE."}

{"id": "a2f05f30-7d9e-42b9-9a8a-f95071484402", "value": "{\"id\": \"bee1733f-ba80-4752-b693-053d30aacb1e\", \"value\": \"Description: \"despite the antiquity of this trade only in the last few centuries BC did it link the area of study [from Middle East to East Asia reaching as far apart as West Africa and the American Pacific coast]\". | Description: 7th - 8th Century AD. Based on chemical analysis Chibuene series beads probably came from the Middle East east of the Euphrates with the Sasanian Persian Gulf trade. Possibly found at Nqoma western Botswana and potentially at sites in East Africa. Around the middle-to-late 10th century importation of Zhizo beads ceased and Chibuene\u2019s role as a port serving Indian Ocean trade and the interior of southern Africa ended. These beads are also found at several sites in West Africa beginning in around the 8th century AD but seem to vanish from trade there by the end of the first millennium AD.\"}"}

{"id": "1399d3ff-a4fd-470d-b7e7-462e55a6e5bc", "value": "A period when Swahili coastal towns were established and flourished. The Swahili coast runs for 3000km from Somalia to Mozambique and is composed of more than 450 urban settlements built initially with mud and later with coral and limestone mortar. These 'urban' settlements were surrounded by fortified stone walls. The architecture of these towns shows Asian Arabi and Indian influences while the material artefacts include exotic items from faraway lands such as China. 700-1600CE | Marked by local Early Iron Age pottery iron and iron slag; 100BCE-300CE"}

{"id": "50547508-2670-4780-9802-77c5e2eb837f", "value": "{\"id\": \"6a6d6a09-dad5-40bb-adcf-aef7a8b1d463\", \"value\": \"Late Period (Phases 4 + 5) : AD 650-1000\" \"Timbuktu\u2019s prehistoric phase (c . 500\u2013400 BC to c . AD 900\u20131000)\" \"The pottery assemblage from Phase 4 changes drastically from Phase 3. At TBZ1 where Phase 4 lies directly on top of Phase 3 the change occurs immediately after the end of Level 5. Simple open rims dominate the assemblage and about 78% of the assemblage is comprised of open vessels. This is a major change from Periods 1 and 2 where the most common type of vessel wad restricted. The most common type of rims is Rim H which makes up 44\u00b5 of the assembkages alone. These rims are long and everted. They often have deep and thick channeling (probably made by fingers as the rim is formed on a slow wheel). This vessel for is used for multiple activities (storage cooking and perhaps serving) and they come in all sizes. Rim H vessels (also known as 'long everted rim vessels\") are all highly constricted at the neck are usually carinated at the widest part of the body and all have rounded bases (see Figures 6.43 and 6.44). Many were found within hearth and other domestic contexts. Others were found associated with grave contexts. Able to be used in multiple circumstances and contexts Rim H vessels semm to be the Swiss-army knife of vessel type found at Tombouze.\" \"It is in Phase 4 that obvious signs of cooking vecome common in the assembkage. About 28% of the vessels from Phase 4 show signs of cooking up from about 5% in either the Early and MIddle Periods. Also the ceramic paste becomes coarser the amount of the fine wares decreases to the lowest numbers observed at Tombouze. The decorative motifs are quite beautiful in Phase 4. Small restricted carinated pots (Rim I) often have triangularly-zoned and sequential bands decorated with the fine comb impressions just above the carination. Overall the quality of Phase 4 pots is quite impressive suggesting that a highly advanced style was brought into the region from somewhere else. However it is too early in our research efforts to suggest where the pottery may have come from\"\"}"}
